videoIdeas.title: You can't speak because you never talk to anyone
videoIdeas.hook: The reason you freeze up when you speak isn't nerves. It's that you haven't had a real conversation in weeks.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your own post 'The amount of people that struggle to string a sentence together is shocking' (616 views, DbilFRjsJ3v) proves you have takes on this, but you underpost public speaking. lifeofdinoo is pulling 6k-14k views on communication content with punchy hooks. This is a gap you own better than anyone because you say it bluntly.
videoIdeas.script: The reason you freeze up when you speak isn't nerves. It's that you haven't had a real conversation in weeks. You've replaced talking to people with reacting to people. A comment here, a voice note there, a story reply. That's not communication, that's noise. Speaking is a muscle. You don't build it by watching me, you build it by going outside and having a conversation you can't edit and can't delete. Order your own coffee. Sit with an elder and actually listen. Disagree with someone to their face without an emoji to soften it. You're not shy. You're just out of practice. Fix that this week.

visuals.setting: Outdoors or in a café, natural light, casual smart clothing, phone slightly below eye level, walking or sitting with relaxed but direct energy — like you're talking to a younger brother across the table.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open on you mid-sentence with on-screen text: 'It's not nerves.' — no intro, straight into the point.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: start by silently miming someone freezing/stuttering, then cut to you speaking clearly
On-screen text punchline that contradicts the expectation: 'Confidence won't fix this'
Cut from a phone screen full of unread chats to your face saying 'this is why you can't talk'

videoIdeas.title: Leadership is competence AND trust, not vibes
videoIdeas.hook: You keep chasing influence. The Prophetic model tells you to chase the opposite first.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your prophetic leadership post (DTauCL6jJ8Z, 508 views, 58 likes — strong like ratio) shows this content resonates with your core followers even if reach was modest. Repackage it with a sharper hook. doctordaanish proves short, direct value-per-line advice for men in their 20s pulls big.
videoIdeas.script: You keep chasing influence. The Prophetic model tells you to chase the opposite first. Al-Qawi wal-Ameen — strong and trustworthy. Notice the order people forget. Everyone wants the platform, the following, the mic. Nobody wants to become the kind of person who can actually be trusted with it. So you get loud people leading who can't be relied on, and reliable people staying silent because they never built the skill. Character before clout. Competence before the crowd. If people can't trust you with something small and private, why would Allah trust you with something big and public. Build the inside first. The influence follows people who don't need it.

visuals.setting: Clean indoor setting, plain wall or bookshelf, seated, calm and deliberate energy — slower delivery than the public speaking one to signal weight.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text appears word by word: 'strong' then 'trustworthy' with a beat between, while you say the hook.
otherHookIdeas: Open on you writing 'Al-Qawi wal-Ameen' on paper/whiteboard then look up
Cold open: 'Everyone wants the mic. Nobody wants this.' then reveal
Split-second freeze on the word 'trust' with on-screen emphasis

videoIdeas.title: Stop performing your Deen online
videoIdeas.hook: If all your posts are about how much money you're making and how holy you've become, you're not practising Deen. You're marketing it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your 'UAE Hijrah bros' post (2106 views, 136 likes) and the 'venom amidst your brothers being attacked' post (1045 views, 109 likes) show your blunt call-out content gets your highest engagement. This turns that same energy inward into a mindset lesson so it's not just refutation — it's self-development.
videoIdeas.script: If all your posts are about how much money you're making and how holy you've become, you're not practising Deen. You're marketing it. There's a difference between doing something for Allah and doing something so people can see you doing it for Allah. And most of us can't tell which one we're on anymore, because the phone rewards the performance and not the sincerity. Ask yourself an uncomfortable question. If nobody could ever see this act — no post, no story, no one clapping — would you still do it? If the answer is no, that's not worship. That's content. Do more that nobody will ever find out about. That's where the real you actually lives.

visuals.setting: Slightly darker, intimate framing, close-up, plain background — the seriousness matches the confrontation. Direct eye contact.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'This one's uncomfortable.' held for a second before you start.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-thought: 'Would you still do it if nobody saw?'
Hold up a phone to the camera, then lower it as you deliver the hook
Text punchline reveal at the end: 'That's not worship. That's content.'

videoIdeas.title: The Ummah doesn't need your hot take today
videoIdeas.hook: Never a boring day when people show me how dumb they can be — arguing over sects while our brothers and sisters are being attacked.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your two highest performers are commentary on unity vs division (protests post 6134 views; 'don't let sectarianism blind you' 827 views/24 comments). This is your proven lane. Frame it as a leadership lesson — priorities and knowing what actually matters — so it fits the pillar and pushes people to act, not just watch.
videoIdeas.script: Never a boring day when people find new ways to show me how dumb they can be. Arguing over sects, over madhabs, over whose scholar said what — while our brothers and sisters are being attacked left, right and centre. Leadership isn't about winning the argument in the comments. It's about knowing what actually deserves your energy today. You have a limited amount of attention. Every ounce you spend tearing down another Muslim online is an ounce you didn't spend on something that's actually dire. The strong ones in this Ummah aren't the loudest debaters. They're the ones who know when to shut up and get to work. Pick your battles like the Ummah is watching. Because it is.

visuals.setting: Direct, slightly heated but controlled energy, plain indoor background, standing, hands used to punctuate — the older brother who's had enough.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text stat/contrast: 'Us:' [arguing emoji] vs 'The situation:' — quick cut into your face.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on a scrolling comment-war screenshot, then cut to you: 'this is what we're doing?'
Pattern interrupt: sigh, look off-camera, then straight into the hook

videoIdeas.title: Third spaces are the leadership move nobody credits
videoIdeas.hook: Young British Muslims quietly built the thing the community's been complaining it doesn't have. And people are mocking it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your third spaces post (872 views, Dbwq4JosFxD) is recent and on a topic competitors aren't touching — a genuine content gap in the niche. Reframe it around leadership: building something is harder than criticising it. This differentiates you from the political-commentary crowd.
videoIdeas.script: Young British Muslims quietly built the thing the community's been complaining it doesn't have. Cafés. Study circles. Community hubs. Actual spaces where people can meet, learn and belong. And instead of backing it, people are online mocking it. Here's what they're missing. Building something is a thousand times harder than criticising it. Anyone can post a paragraph about what the Ummah lacks. Very few will spend two years and their own money making a room where a lonely brother can walk in and feel like he belongs. That's leadership. Not the title, not the mic — the willingness to build the thing everyone else only talks about. If you see young people doing that, you don't dunk on it. You show up and you help.

visuals.setting: Filmed in or near an actual café / community space if possible, warmer tone, walking-and-talking energy, brighter and more hopeful than your call-out videos.
visuals.visualHook: B-roll of a busy café/study circle for 1.5 seconds with text 'They built this.' before cutting to you.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open: 'They're mocking the best thing we've done in years.'
Gesture to the space around you as the hook lands

videoIdeas.title: You're not busy, you're avoiding the hard hour
videoIdeas.hook: You say you don't have time. You have time. You just spend it on things that don't scare you.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your 'trivialise vs leisure and work' post (884 views, DaYdhqOMm3K) touched discipline but got 0 comments — the idea was there, the hook wasn't. Repackage as a sharp mindset piece. birdtart and doctordaanish prove short 20s-advice mindset content scales; you can do it without the soft coaching tone.
videoIdeas.script: You say you don't have time. You have time. You just spend it on the things that don't scare you. Scrolling doesn't scare you. Replying to messages doesn't scare you. The gym you already know how to do doesn't scare you. But the one hour of real work — the memorisation, the difficult book, the skill you're bad at, the thing that makes you feel stupid at the start — that one you keep 'not having time' for. Be honest. It's not a schedule problem. It's a fear problem dressed up as a busy problem. Everyone can distinguish leisure from work. The difference between people who go somewhere and people who don't is whether they'll sit in the hard hour when it's uncomfortable. Find your hard hour today. Sit in it.

visuals.setting: Simple, focused setting — desk with a book/notebook visible, or plain wall. Lower energy, more matter-of-fact, like calling out a lie gently but firmly.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'You have time.' appears immediately, contradicting the excuse people expect you to validate.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open holding up a phone showing screen time, then set it down
Pattern interrupt: 'Stop lying to yourself for one second.'
Text punchline close: 'Sit in the hard hour.'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post ever — 6134 views, 211 likes. The reason: a timely, unapologetic stance ('Can't believe we're still discussing the necessity of protests in 2026') that gives people something to agree with and share. The blunt older-brother voice is at its sharpest here and the topic is urgent, so people showed up.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The caption cuts off mid-sentence ('feel bett...') which kills the emotional payoff for anyone reading before watching. Front-load the strongest line and finish the thought within the first two lines so the caption itself is shareable even muted. Also add one clear question to drive the 15 comments higher — this reach deserved more conversation.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 827 views but 24 comments — one of your highest comment counts. 'Don't let sectarianism blind you to the horrors that occurred in our Ummah' is short, absolute and touches a nerve, so people felt compelled to respond. Short declarative captions are outperforming your long ones for engagement.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: High comments, low likes (42) suggests it sparked debate more than agreement — some of those comments may be pushback. Add a line that gives the people who agree with you something to rally behind, not just a statement that invites argument. Channel the debate toward a shared conclusion instead of leaving it open-ended.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your clearest public-speaking content and the premise is strong — 'people struggle to string a sentence together' is a hook with teeth. It's the pillar you're most underusing, so it fills a gap.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 616 views and 0 comments — the lowest engagement despite a good idea. Two problems: the caption buries the point under 'I'm not saying everyone should be a public speaker,' softening your own hook, and there's no ask. Lead with the blunt line, cut the hedging, and end with a direct question like 'when's the last time you had a conversation you couldn't edit?' to force replies.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 2106 views, 136 likes — your third-best reach and a very strong like-to-view ratio. The 'UAE Hijrah bros' call-out is specific, names a real behaviour, and takes a clear side. Specific targets outperform vague ones every time; people knew exactly what you meant.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 5 comments for that reach — the take was so complete it left nothing to add. Leave one deliberate open door: ask 'am I wrong?' or 'tell me I'm misreading it' so the people who half-agree jump in. Also the caption trails off ('brag ab...'); tighten it so the punch lands inside two lines.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 508 views but 58 likes — one of your best like ratios, meaning your core audience genuinely values this. 'We chase influence before character' and 'Al-Qawi wal-Ameen, competent and trustworthy' is exactly the leadership content the brief is built around, and it landed with the people who matter.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 1 comment and modest reach — the hook is a statement, not a snag. Rewrite the opening as a challenge ('You're chasing the wrong thing first') and shorten the caption; the Surah reference and '11 Prophetic Qualities' list feel like a carousel caption on a video. Pick one quality per video and go deep so each has a single, punchy takeaway that travels.
